passage: Every Sunday in Seoul, Paulo made feijoada in a pot far too big for his tiny studio: black beans soaked overnight, garlic filling the corridor. At noon he propped his phone against the rice cooker and video-called his mother in Recife, where it was just past midnight and she was cooking the same dish. They compared bubbles and laughed. This year, for the first time, he invited people too: Soo-ah from his lab, her roommate, and the old man downstairs who always asked about the smell. Soo-ah brought kimchi. The old man brought rice wine and stayed three hours. When Paulo's mother saw them all squeezed onto his floor, she clapped. 'You have a family there too!'

qa.a: Against the rice cooker.

qa.q: What might Paulo feel when his mother says "You have a family there too!"?
qa.a: Paulo probably feels warm and relieved, seeing that keeping home alive and making friends in Seoul can go together. 😊

qa.a: Paulo invited Soo-ah, her roommate and the neighbour to the Sunday meal, turning a private ritual into a way to build friendships where he lives.

qa.q: What might the Sunday meal mean to the old man downstairs?
qa.a: The old man, who always asked about the smell, may feel welcomed and less lonely, which is perhaps why he stayed three hours.

grounding: A young man abroad keeps a weekly home dish and video call with his mother, and this year shares it with new local friends.

passage: In the nurses' break room at the hospital in Chennai, Lalremsiami unpacked a steel box of bai, the Mizo vegetable stew her mother had taught her over the phone. It was Chapchar Kut back home in Aizawl; her family would be dancing in the square tonight. She had a video call booked for nine, after her shift. Shalini, the senior nurse, sniffed the air. "What is that? It smells like my grandmother's keerai." "Try it," Lalremsiami said, handing her a spoon. By the end of the break four nurses were eating from the box, and Shalini was explaining how her family makes keerai. Lalremsiami laughed. She still missed Aizawl, a quiet ache. But she had started learning Tamil, and next January Shalini was taking her home for Pongal.

qa.q: What time was Lalremsiami's video call booked for?
qa.a: For nine, after her shift.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami feel about Aizawl while sharing the stew?
qa.a: Lalremsiami still misses Aizawl with a quiet ache, but the warmth of sharing the stew keeps her in the present.

qa.q: Which of Lalremsiami's choices helps most, and why?
qa.a: Sharing the festival food with colleagues turns homesickness into connection, while the booked call keeps family close.

qa.q: What might the shared break mean to Shalini?
qa.a: Shalini is reminded of her grandmother's cooking and gets to share her own family's recipes, which builds a real friendship.

grounding: A nurse far from home keeps a festival dish and family call alive while building friendships with colleagues where she works.

passage:
Dear Zainab Apa,
Eid in Leeds was not like home, but it wasn't sad either, so don't worry.
I woke early and made sheer khurma the way Ammi does, burning the vermicelli only a little. We video-called at noon, you remember, everyone shouting at once and Abbu's face too close to the camera. I cried after, just for a minute, missing the sound of the whole mohalla on Eid morning.
Then I took the leftovers to the common room in my building. Wanjiru from Kenya, Tom from Wales and the Polish girls upstairs came. None of them had tasted sheer khurma. Tom had three bowls.
I'm keeping Hyderabad in my kitchen, Apa, and making a little home here too. Both fit.
Your Rehana

qa.q: What did Rehana make on Eid morning?
qa.a: Sheer khurma, the way Ammi does.

qa.q: Why did Rehana cry for a minute after the call?
qa.a: Rehana was missing the sounds and togetherness of Eid morning at home, even though the call itself was joyful.

qa.q: What did Rehana choose to do after crying, and how did it help?
qa.a: Rehana took the leftovers to the common room and shared them with new friends, letting the longing turn into connection in Leeds.

qa.q: How might Zainab Apa feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Zainab Apa would likely feel relieved that Rehana isn't lonely, and proud that Ammi's recipe is making a home abroad.

grounding: A young adult abroad keeps an Eid dish and family call alive and shares the festival meal with new friends.

subtype: Carrying home while building a new one [Response]
passage:
"Saurabh, you've been in Leeds two weeks, right? Okay, listen, because I did everything wrong my first year in Berlin.
I kept Pune alive in my room like a museum. Every Sunday I'd video-call Aai and Baba for two hours, and then feel empty all evening. I said no to every invite.
Then at Gudi Padwa in my second year I thought, fine, let's try. I made puran poli, badly, and put up a small gudi on the balcony with a steel lota on top. And I invited my flatmate Lena and two women from the office. They didn't know what anything meant, so I explained, and hearing myself explain it made it feel alive again. Aai watched the whole thing on video and kept shouting, 'Sonali, my girl, fold it tighter!'
Now I still call every Sunday, but shorter. I also play football with the office team on Thursdays. Home keeps me warm. It doesn't have to be the only fire, you know?"

qa.q: What did Sonali put on top of the gudi?
qa.a: She put a steel lota on top.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel after her long Sunday calls in the first year?
qa.a: She felt empty all evening, because the calls kept home in front of her while she had nothing in Berlin to return to.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Sonali, and what did it change?
qa.a: At Gudi Padwa she chose to cook, put up a gudi and invite Lena and colleagues; sharing the festival made it feel alive and opened her to friendships where she lived.

qa.q: If you were Saurabh, two weeks into Leeds, what might you take from Sonali's story?
qa.a: Saurabh might feel relieved that missing home is normal, and see that calls and traditions can stay while still saying yes to invitations in Leeds.

grounding: It shows an adult who keeps a festival, a meal and calls with her parents while also making friends where she lives, so home warms her without holding her back.

passage:
I'm Pankaj, a retired man on the second floor, Block C, here in Ludhiana. Uma moved in opposite us last June, from somewhere in Tamil Nadu, I think Madurai.
The first thing I noticed was the kolam. Every morning, rice-flour patterns outside her door, even in the fog of December. My wife says she does it at six, still in her shawl.
In January she knocked on every door on our landing with steel boxes of sweet pongal. She said it was her festival and she didn't want to eat it alone. My son now asks for it by name.
Some evenings I see her on the stairs, talking fast in Tamil on a video call, laughing, sometimes quiet afterwards. I can't say what she feels then. Maybe she misses home more than she lets on.
But she also joined the colony walking group, and last Lohri she was the one feeding sticks into the bonfire, clapping along to songs she didn't know.

qa.q: What did Uma bring to every door on the landing in January?
qa.a: She brought steel boxes of sweet pongal.

qa.q: What does Pankaj think Uma might be feeling when she goes quiet after her calls?
qa.a: He guesses she may be homesick, missing home more than she lets on, though he says he cannot be sure what she feels.

qa.q: Which of Uma's choices helped her most in the new place, and why?
qa.a: Sharing her pongal and joining the walking group and the Lohri bonfire let her keep her own customs while becoming part of the colony, instead of keeping home only to herself.

qa.q: How has Uma's arrival affected Pankaj's family?
qa.a: It has warmed them: his wife notices her early kolam, his son now asks for pongal by name, and Pankaj watches her with friendly interest and some care.

grounding: It shows, through a neighbour's eyes, an adult who keeps her rituals, festival food and calls home while also joining the life of the colony where she now lives.
